Record date: 2130-01-23
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 01/23/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Continued shortness of breath and cough, with persistent fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for follow-up after two days of outpatient management following his previous hospitalization for COPD exacerbation and pneumonia. The patient reports slight improvement in his respiratory symptoms since the transition to oral Amoxicillin/Clavulanate. He notes a reduction in the frequency of his cough, though it remains productive with yellowish-green sputum. Mr. Fairfax still experiences significant dyspnea, particularly during exertion, and reports ongoing fatigue, which he attributes to both his respiratory condition and the corticosteroid therapy.
During this visit, Mr. Fairfax mentions that he has been adhering to his medication regimen but has developed mild epigastric discomfort, which he believes may be associated with the Prednisone. He denies any new fevers or chills but continues to experience night sweats.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + persistent fatigue, - new fevers, + night sweats, - weight loss. Pulmonary - + improved cough, + persistent productive cough with yellowish-green sputum, + wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + mild epigastric discomfort, - nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 128/75 mmHg - Heart Rate: 90 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 26 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 87% on supplemental oxygen (6 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued but is in moderate respiratory distress, utilizing accessory muscles for breathing.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Moderate wheezing on auscultation; decreased breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with rhonchi; crackles audible, particularly in the lower lung fields.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender; mild epigastric discomfort noted; no hepatosplenomegaly.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with ongoing bacterial pneumonia, evidenced by persistent respiratory symptoms and suboptimal response to current antibiotic therapy. 2. Mild hypoxemia requiring adjustment of oxygen therapy; patient shows slight improvement in oxygen saturation. 3. Fatigue likely exacerbated by systemic steroid therapy and unresolved respiratory pathology, with new onset of mild gastrointestinal discomfort likely related to Prednisone.
PLAN
1. Continue oral Amoxicillin/Clavulanate 875 mg every 12 hours and reassess clinical response in 48 hours; consider switching to a different antibiotic if no improvement is noted. 2. Maintain oral Prednisone at 80 mg daily but initiate a taper to 60 mg daily due to the development of mild epigastric discomfort; prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (Omeprazole 20 mg daily) to mitigate gastric irritation. 3. Adjust supplemental oxygen to 6 L via nasal cannula and monitor oxygen saturation closely; consider a trial of BiPAP if significant hypoxemia persists. 4. Schedule a repeat chest X-ray to evaluate for any new complications or resolution of pneumonia; consider obtaining a sputum culture if symptoms do not improve. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed; increase frequency if wheezing persists; consider adding Ipratropium bromide for enhanced bronchodilation. 6. Schedule a follow-up visit within 48 hours to reassess respiratory status and medication efficacy; discuss the potential for pulmonary rehabilitation once stabilized.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax remains under close observation in the internal medicine unit. The treatment team will continue to adjust the management plan based on his clinical progress, particularly focusing on his respiratory function and gastrointestinal symptoms. Patient education regarding medication adherence and the importance of reporting any new or worsening symptoms will be emphasized during this visit.
